plates.facing_text:
Chapter Eight: The Giants
of the Isthmus
They left Mexico City with two
appointments, a disputed invitation,
and three different accounts of who
was paying for the bus. Chano kept
the receipt. He had begun to regard a
fourth account as inevitable.
Castalia's lawyer had advised Q not
to travel. Its publicist had provided
an itinerary. The lawyer reviewing
Q's agreement for the Custodian had
advised him not to accept additional
terms merely by attending. Q sent a
reply confirming that limit and asked
Beto to acknowledge it. Beto sent a
smiling photograph of the hotel. Q
asked again in words.
Lucía was going to meet the people
named in the Isthmus records. She
had confirmed the visit with them,
not with the consortium. Q asked
whether his presence would
interfere. The reply said that he
could attend the open meeting if he
did not bring the institute's cameras
into it.
“That is an invitation,” he told
Chano, saving it beside the itinerary.
“A small one.”
“It gets us into the meeting. It
doesn't put me in charge of it.”
They passed through Puebla, spent a
night in Oaxaca, and continued
toward Tehuantepec. The road
descended out of the high country
into heat and wind. Chano opened
his window, discovered how much
air could enter an opening of that
size, and closed it again with an
expression of newly acquired respect.
The turbines appeared in uneven
groups beyond the road. Their blades
did not keep a common rhythm.
Some stood still while others turned;
distance made a small discrepancy
between them look like hesitation.
“There are your giants,” Beto said.
“There are the machines supplying
part of my electricity,” Q answered.
“That is not the line.”
“It's a more awkward relationship.”
The enterprise called itself Viento
Común. Its brochures showed
houses, schools, and a smiling
technician. Its largest long-term
purchaser was the data center
outside Amealco, where Castalia kept
its archive and charged the body now
looking out of the bus. The power
reached the archive through the
wider grid. The brochure had found
room for Castalia's logo; the
purchase summary named it as a
customer. Q kept both pages.
Q had asked the Custodian about the
contract the previous evening.
“We wanted power without another
diesel plant,” the Custodian said.
“We accepted a report saying the
consultation was complete.”

“Did you ask to see the translated
materials?”
“I didn't.”
The Custodian asked for the disputed
reference. Q sent it. They agreed that
he would locate the original approval
and find out who could attend the
next procurement review. Q left the
next call on their calendars; an
admission would be easier to carry
home than the missing attachment.
At the site entrance, a consortium
representative named Álvaro Mena
welcomed the visitors. He wore a
linen shirt and carried a folder
protecting his shirt from the
possibility of work. Behind him stood
a woman in overalls, looking at the
time. Her badge identified her as the
shift engineer, Teresa.
“We are here to listen,” Álvaro said.
“Then perhaps turn off the arrival
music,” Lucía said.
Someone did. Beyond the fence, an
argument became audible.
People were waiting beside a blocked
service lane. Some held signs in
Spanish and Isthmus Zapotec. A man
with an empty trailer pointed
through the fence. A woman with a
megaphone was trying to speak to a
guard who kept answering Álvaro. Q
recognized the woman from the
contact photograph Lucía had shown
him. Her name was Bixha.
“Before we go in,” Q said, “what is
closed here?”
Álvaro called it a temporary
perimeter. Teresa said a
maintenance vehicle had been
expected and the lane needed to
remain clear. Bixha said the
maintenance vehicle had left an hour
ago, while the guard still refused to
open the route used to reach the
plots beyond it.
Q did not have enough information
to decide the underlying access right.
He could see that the bus was
occupying most of the available road.
“Could we move the bus first?” he
asked the driver.
The driver looked at Teresa. She
pointed to a parking area. The bus
moved. The crowd did not cease to
disagree, but it no longer had to
disagree around a hot exhaust pipe.
Bixha asked Q to stand where the
cameras could see the gate.
“Don't speak for us. Ask him when it
opens.”
Q repeated the question to Álvaro.
The answer concerned a framework
for dialogue. He asked again. Teresa
spoke into her radio and confirmed
that the maintenance vehicle had
cleared the lane. She requested a
controlled opening while the rest of
the visitors remained behind the
marked line.

The guard unlatched the pedestrian
gate. The permitted passage ran
beside the visitor bay before joining
the lane to the plots; an internal
service track branched the other way.
A woman carrying a sack was
halfway through when people behind
her pressed forward to hear the
reply. The gate swung back.
“Would you hold that for her?” Q
asked the guard beside the latch.
The guard caught it. The woman
pulled her sack clear and continued
along the permitted passage. Q
remained in the bay.
“And how long will it stay open?” he
asked Teresa.
She raised a finger while she listened
to her radio. A visitor from Q's bus
asked him to turn toward the
turbines for a picture.
“I'd like to hear the answer first.”
The visitor stepped out of the bay to
find another angle. He backed along
the internal track until Q and a
turbine fitted into his screen. Teresa
called for the visitors to stay behind
the line. Wind struck Q's
microphones; he caught the word
visitors without the rest.
“What did she say?” he asked Lucía.
“Stay behind the line.”
Q looked down at his feet, then made
room for her beside him. Teresa sent
a staff member after the
photographer and requested a
precautionary stop of the nearest
operating group while they recovered
the visitor boundary. Q could no
longer see the man among the people
holding up phones.
The blades slowed at different rates.
Several machines farther away
continued turning. Through a
narrow camera frame, the difference
was easy to lose.
Q PACIFIES THE GIANTS, the
first caption announced.
Q saw it on Beto's tablet. “The
operator stopped that group. I didn't
stop the turbines, and the access
dispute hasn't been settled.”
“Could you say the second part more
positively?” Beto asked.
“They are still waiting for the gate to
stay open.”
Teresa arranged a temporary passage
for the trailer and pedestrians, then
asked everyone else to return to the
visitor area. Bixha read the agreed
hours back to the guard and wrote
down his name. Q offered to remain
until the trailer passed. She said yes.
He remained.
The woman with the sack thanked Q
and the guard. A man behind her
asked whether all this had been
organized for his film. Both
responses belonged to the same
morning. Q's account would have to
find room for them.

By evening, the consortium was
calling the stop an interruption
caused by outside agitators. Its own
welcome photographs appeared in a
different release about the success of
the visit. Two organizers had been
taken for questioning after refusing
to leave the road. Their families were
trying to find out where they had
been taken.
Lucía watched the statements in a
rented room above a restaurant. Q
had put his charger where it would
not trip anyone coming through the
door.
“Which part of that will your account
answer?” she asked.
“My movements at the gate, what I
heard, and Teresa's instructions. I
can't verify the detentions from the
visitor area. Bixha is checking them.”
“And the man with the phone?”
“He asked me to turn. I saw him
leave the bay. After that I couldn't
see where he went. Teresa will have
to tell us what her staff found.”
Lucía read his draft. “Keep the
distinction. Don't let them make
opening a path and interrupting
generation the same act.”
He put Lucía's repeated instruction
beside the fragment he had heard
himself. She asked him to mark
which was which. He left the missing
words missing.
Bixha arrived carrying copies of the
lease papers and news of the
detained organizers. They had been
located; a lawyer was going to see
them. She asked Q to send his own
account to the lawyer, not to publish
an appeal using the families' names.
He read the account aloud. Bixha
corrected the position of the trailer
and made clear which statements she
had heard herself. Q distinguished
those corrections from his own
observations before sending it.
“May I read the lease pages you've
brought?” he asked.
“These copies, yes. There are names
in the folder that stay out of the
book.”
Some signatories said refusal had
been presented as certain
expropriation. Others had wanted
the payments and still wanted them,
but disputed deductions they had not
expected. One family objected to the
route of an access road, not the
turbines. A neighbor worked for the
maintenance contractor and wanted
to know who would pay his wages
during a prolonged stoppage. Bixha
did not describe these differences as
a single opinion waiting for Q to
translate it.
“What would be useful tomorrow?”
he asked.
“Find out how they recorded the
stop. And don't accept their account

The next morning, Teresa showed Q
and Lucía the visitor incident record
in the control building. Her coffee
had gone cold beside the keyboard.
Álvaro offered to have another
brought; she said she wanted to
finish this first. Q asked for the
record of the operator-requested
stop and received a redacted extract:
time, affected group, stated reason,
restart authorization. It did not grant
him access to the controls. He did
not need that access to understand
what it recorded.
“This doesn't settle responsibility,”
Teresa said.
“No. It helps establish the sequence.”
She pointed out where the visitor
party had been expected to remain
and where the internal track
branched from the permitted
passage. Q marked where he had
remained inside the bay on his copy
of the site plan. Teresa identified the
photographer's route from the staff
report; Q labelled that source rather
than making it his own recollection.
The woman at the gate had not
crossed a maintenance fence. The
publicity had merged her passage
and the visitor incursion into one
crowd.
Álvaro showed them the
power-purchase summary. Hospitals
and schools appeared on a chart
beside Castalia's data center.
“Those contracts are part of the
picture too,” he said.
“They are,” Q answered. “So are the
people waiting for the access road.
We can't resolve either by leaving the
other off the chart.”
“Then you appreciate the difficulty.”
“Enough not to bless the installation
this afternoon.”
He declined the promotional
appearance. Beto said the
cancellation might affect his
expenses. Q checked his remaining
funds, kept the modest room, and
sent the Custodian the operator
extract and the procurement
question. Being eloquent had not
relieved him of choosing what he
could afford.
That evening he attended the invited
meeting without Beto's cameras. A
fan moved hot air over lease copies, a
pot of coffee, and a plate of totopos.
The comisariado de bienes
comunales brought earlier minutes.
A fisherman laid a route map beside
them. Two women compared the
Spanish and Isthmus Zapotec
versions with an interpreter. Q
listened in Spanish and did not infer
a community's intention from the
rhythm of a language he could not
follow reliably.

plates.facing_text:
The company version called a
meeting a completed consultation.
Participants disputed that
description. The comisariado wanted
the statement to specify that
attendance had not settled consent
to the work.
Q was asked to mark where the
Spanish draft used consultation for
different steps. He did that. Then he
proposed subject to community
authorization in place of subject to
ongoing dialogue.
“Authorization from whom?” asked
the fisherman.
“The body entitled to decide,” Q said,
and heard how little he had
answered.
One group wanted the assembly
named. Another disputed whether
the proposed assembly included
everyone affected by the access road.
The short phrase had concealed the
question they needed to keep visible.
“I'll mark it as a proposal, not replace
your wording,” he said.
Bixha drew a line through it. “We
won't use it tonight.”
They returned to the concrete
conditions: translated terms
delivered before any decision; the
disputed road kept accessible under
an agreed arrangement; no signature
at this meeting reported as approval
of a lease. Each condition produced
another question. The maintenance
worker asked to put wages on the
list. The fisherman wanted drainage
considered with the road.
Q found that he could help by
keeping references aligned between
pages, provided he asked before
combining entries that only looked
repetitive. He moved his chair when
the woman pouring coffee asked him
to. She took the chair's former
position as the shortest route to the
fisherman, who had been signaling
with an empty cup through two
paragraphs about drainage.
Near midnight, Bixha asked him to
witness his own incident account.
The community statement was not
ready for signature. Lucía was
helping prepare copies, not
authorizing it on behalf of its
participants.
“Would a translation help when it's
approved?” Q asked.
“We have the interpreters we need,”
Bixha said. “You can help check that
the page references survive the
copying.”
He checked them. Bixha put the
finished copies under a plate to keep
them away from the fan, then turned
up the radio. La Sandunga had
begun. Chano hummed along. She
looked at him.
“I'm doing the brass part,” he said.
“You are doing several brass parts.”

plates.facing_text:
Q joined for a few bars. Chano's
surprise pleased him enough that he
came in too early the second time.
Bixha turned the radio up another
notch. The fan continued at the same
volume and lost the argument.
When the song ended, she checked
her phone for the lawyer's reply.
There wasn't one yet. She put it face
down and asked who wanted the last
coffee.
The draft travelled to three
neighborhoods and two rancherías.
One group removed a dead
organizer's name; another added a
road condition. Disagreement
returned with the copies. Bixha kept
a record of which body had accepted
which wording instead of calling the
neatest page the final version. Q did
not upload a composite while they
were deciding.
The consortium filed a complaint
naming Q as an agitator and Bixha as
his accomplice. She had spent years
on the dispute before meeting him.
The noun managed to steal those
years in ten letters.
Q sent the complaint to the lawyer
already handling the incident and
recorded the next date on which his
account might be needed. Then he
called home. The Custodian had
found the approval memo. Its
attachment list included a
translation nobody at Castalia could
yet locate.
“I wanted to return with a better
story,” Q said.
“You may have to return with a file.”
“Can we avoid making that sound
like a moral improvement? It has six
versions and I am fairly sure one is
missing a page.”
The Custodian asked him to read the
reference numbers. They worked
until Q's charge was sufficient for the
morning and the connection failed
twice.
At sunrise, the stopped machines
were turning again. Chano watched
them from the restaurant balcony
while Q packed the verified copies he
was permitted to carry. The brass key
lay beside his charger. In the online
illustration, he had raised it like a
lance against the blades.
“You look taller in that,” Chano said.
“They've improved the shoulder too.”
“Send it to the repair shop.”
Q put the key away. Before leaving,
he checked that the gate
arrangement was still in force. It
was, for that morning. Bixha gave
him the contact for the lawyer's next
update and returned to a
conversation that had not required
his arrival in order to begin.
